sentences.text: Four special situations to finish the towing rule.
First, a tow that severely restricts the tug’s ability to deviate from her course.
She adds the lights and shapes of a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver, on top of her towing lights.
Remember the ladder: that moves her up near the top.
Second, things that are hard to see.
An inconspicuous, partly submerged vessel or object being towed, like a fuel bladder, shows all-round white lights at its ends, more if it’s very wide, and a diamond shape at the after end.
Third, what if the tow simply can’t be lit that way?
Then all possible measures shall be taken to light it, or at least to show that it’s there.
And fourth, this one is about you.
Say a friend’s boat breaks down at dusk and you take her in tow.
You’re not a towing vessel, and you don’t carry towing lights.
A vessel not normally engaged in towing needn’t show towing lights when it’s impracticable.
But you must show the connection between the two boats, for example by lighting up the towline.
Yellow over white from astern, two or three white lights stacked from ahead, and two yellow lights for an Inland pusher.
Next time: sailboats and fishing vessels.
